You should automate a task if the benefit is higher than the cost of automating it. That’s always been true, but a fundamental part of this equation has completely changed in the last year. I used to think twice before writing scripts to automate repetitive work because it would take a while. Most tasks didn’t feel common enough to bother automating. What’s Changed in the Last Year Code generation models and agentic tooling (like Codex or Claude Code - not an ad) have completely changed this for me this year. Now, automating work is almost free. I automate just about everything if it’s easy to access from the terminal. Some examples: 1. Podcast transcript processing: Problem: Audio transcription for my podcast is not accurate and needs fixing. LLMs can fix these but can’t handle the entire 2-hour transcript all at once. Solution: Generated a script to chunk up the transcript and feed it to an LLM API. One command, done. 2. Rescuing podcast footage: Problem: I use software to record remote podcasts. It uploads the video in chunks, but for one interview the uploads failed. We couldn’t fix it, but we found all the video chunks in his Chrome folder. So he sent me a zip with hundreds of numbered files containing the video chunks. Solution: Generated a script to list and sort the files, then used ffmpeg to stitch it all together. Note: Even though this isn’t a task I expect to do again, generating the script was still easier than figuring out the ffmpeg command by hand. 3. Moving notes to Markdown Problem: I wanted to use Obsidian, but my notes were scattered in many file formats across Google Docs, Apple Notes, and Google Keep. Solution: Dumped all exported zips in one place and wrote three scripts, one for each format, to convert to Markdown. Note: Again, this isn’t something I’ll do again yet generating a script was the fastest way. In the past, I wouldn’t have done the migration, but now it’s so easy I figured why not. This has changed how I use my computer fundamentally. I automate a lot more because the cost is basically zero. I have AI write quick one-off scripts for me more often than I do these small local tasks myself. Not only do these agentic tools save me time, they let me do things I wouldn’t have done before because they weren’t worth the trouble. LLM code generation isn’t perfect, but for these small, targeted tasks it’s actually great. LLMs are likely to get it right the first time, and even if not, being wrong doesn’t matter much. Verifier/generator gap scaling means the verifier must stay ahead of the generator. There were impulses sparking around my edges: the urge to check my phone the reflex to scroll, the familiar tug to look for signs in any of the men who have played roles in my myth or to stress about my material situation which is still unresolved or to start cataloguing everything as my mind tried to do yesterday. But each impulse rose and fell without catching me. I didn’t follow any of them. I didn’t push them away either. I just watched them appear like small sparks that flickered then dissolved back into the field. I chose instead to continue sitting in silence, letting everything move through me into the grass. Focusing on sensations the sound of birds the breeze on my skin the sway of the trees the texture of the world around me the beads of dew gather on dainty spiderwebs the way light scatters and glints and disappears as clouds drift overhead. Not trusting in the confident way I’ve felt at other times that everything will work out~ but knowing quietly deep in the body that this is the only thing to do right now. No problem-solving no reaching no searching for signals no forcing clarity no narrative. Just this. Just the sensation of being here while the psyche re-shelves itself behind the scenes, books returning to their rightful places in an order I can’t see yet but can feel settling one subtle click at a time.
